title: The greatest gift
hook: above all, the gift of the Name

segments.voice: Yesterday: gifts asked for, and your line: ask for faith. Which gift did you need, and did you ask for it? Yesterday's list had six gifts. Today, the seventh, the one at the head of the list. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

On some strings of prayer beads, one bead is different from the rest. It's bigger, or set apart, or has a tassel. You start from it and you finish at it; your fingers know when they've reached it without looking. The Ardas's list of gifts works the same way. Sikhi, kes, rahit, bibek, visaah, bharosaa: six gifts, each one precious. And then one more, and the Ardas marks it out from all the others with a single phrase, so that no one could mistake which one matters most. Today: the greatest gift.
screen: `ONE BEAD IS DIFFERENT.` → `YOUR FINGERS KNOW IT.` → `ONE GIFT, SET APART.`

segments.voice: After the six gifts, the Ardas says: daanaan sir daan, naam daan. The gift at the head of all gifts: the gift of the Name. Sir is the head, the top, the crown. So the phrase means the gift that crowns the others, the one all the rest are under. Naam daan. Naam, the Name, you've met many times on this path. It isn't only a word for God. It's God's presence, known and remembered, filling a life. Why is it above discipline, discernment, trust and faith? Because, Sikhs would say, it's the source of them. Remember the Khalsa's prayer from two days ago: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that, every joy. And Guru Tegh Bahadur's last salok: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The Ardas is saying the same thing a third way. Of everything that can be given, the Ardas names this one to ask for and want most. The word daan has a second edge, too. Here it means a gift received. But Gurbani also groups three words, naam, daan, ishnaan: the Name, giving, and cleansing. There, daan means giving to others. So the Name is a gift you receive, and a life of giving is how it shows. Some Sikhs also speak of the amrit ceremony as receiving naam daan, the gift of the Name from the Panj Pyare. Whether in a ceremony or in the quiet of a morning, in the Ardas it's asked for as a gift. In this teaching, nobody earns the Name. They ask for it, and they receive it.
screen: `DAANAAN SIR DAAN: THE CROWN OF GIFTS.` · `NAAM: GOD'S PRESENCE, REMEMBERED.` · `THE SOURCE OF THE OTHER SIX.` · `RECEIVED AS A GIFT, SHOWN IN GIVING.` · then, large: `THE NAME ABOVE ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for the Name. Sit and let your breath slow. Picture a string of beads in your hand, and let your fingers find the one that's different. If you pray, you can ask simply for naam daan, the gift of the Name, and then say Waheguru slowly, letting it fill the time. If you don't, ask yourself what you'd want at the head of your own list, the one gift you'd put above the others, and sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Naam daan. Daanaan sir daan: the gift at the head of all gifts, the gift of the Name.
Your line: the name above all. When today's list feels long, ask what sits at the head of it, and start there. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: At the end of the Ardas's list of gifts, Sikhs ask for daanaan sir daan naam daan, the gift of the Name above all gifts; some also speak of receiving naam at the amrit ceremony.

fork.setup: you can ask for only one gift today: discipline, discernment, trust, or the Name. which does the Ardas put first?
options: discipline, because it keeps the others.
the Name, because the others come from it.

original.note: Gurmukhi: naam daan, the gift of the Name, called the gift at the head of all gifts.

trapdoor: what you thought: naam daan is the last item on a list.
what it means: it's the crown of the list, the gift the other gifts flow from.
what a scholar hears: sir (head) marks it as chief; Gurbani's triad naam daan ishnaan uses daan for giving, so the word carries both receiving and giving.
